About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Physical Education Year 11 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Physical Education Year 11 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Physical Education Year 11 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Physical Education Year 11 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from
1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January
2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.




Physical Education | Year 11 | October 2026                                               Page 2

Purpose statement                                           He oranga ngākau, he pikinga waiora.   Positive feelings in your heart will raise your sense of self-worth.




  In Physical Education, students are taught functional anatomy, exercise
  physiology, biomechanics, and skill learning as they relate to participation and
  performance in physical activity. Physical Education includes studying how
  sociocultural influences, leadership, coaching, and the psychology of movement
  shape inclusive, adaptive, and performance-focused physical activity
  experiences. Students are taught how to apply theoretical, scientific, and practical
  knowledge across a range of physical activities, games, and sports to analyse the
  social and cultural influences on participation and performance, including how
  physical activity contributes to overall well-being.

Students are taught to explain how movement is produced, learned, adapted, and
experienced using concepts from functional anatomy, exercise physiology,
biomechanics, skill learning, movement psychology, leadership, and sociocultural
perspectives. They analyse how performance, participation, and well-being are
influenced by physical, environmental, and social factors.
Physical Education provides students with the knowledge and practices to analyse
performance and apply disciplinary concepts in physical activity contexts. Students
refine movement and tactical strategies, apply mental skills and leadership
approaches, and evaluate learning processes and participation experiences using
reflective, evidence-informed reasoning.
As students progress through Year 11, they develop the ability to explain and analyse
physical activity, strategies, and training principles, and evaluate performance
decisions in written form. This enables them to communicate conclusions and justify
decisions that support safe and inclusive participation.

  Physical Education leads to pathways in sport sciences, sport coaching and
  leadership, health and physical activity promotion, community health, fitness, and
  sport performance.

 Disciplinary writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.

 In Physical Education, writing is an analytical and reflective practice, enabling students to use subject-specific concepts and terminology to construct clear, reasoned explanations
 of performance, well-being, and training. Through writing, students evaluate performance and justify decisions, while reflection, goal setting, and purposeful note-making operate
 as ongoing processes that track progress, deepen thinking, and inform continuous improvement.

The teaching of all knowledge and practices is compulsory. However, schools can
determine how learning is organised across the year, including integrating content
from multiple elements and strands where this supports coherence and depth.
Examples within the teaching sequence in brackets signified with ‘e.g.’ are provided
as guidance only; as long as the intended knowledge and practices are met, schools
and teachers may substitute contexts and examples that better reflect local
environments, iwi and hapū connections, student interests, and teacher expertise.

Disciplinary writing is included in the teaching sequence to set out what subject-
specific literacy is to be taught. It is organised into a knowledge component that is
consistent across all year levels and a practice component sequenced across years.
